Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: If you conduct any published research, do you publish it through open access?
Answer: Yes, whenever possible. In particular, I regularly post versions of my papers (1) to my own personal web site and (2) to arXiv. So even if the official publication venue is not open-access, there are open-access versions of the paper available. I’ve published about 100 papers over the last 30 years; not one publisher has ever objected (or, I suspect, even noticed). I have never paid to have a paper published open-access. But over time, more and more conferences and journals are switching to either diamond open access or limited-time paywalls, so it’s usually easy to steer away from venues whose publishers use permanent locks. There are exceptions—papers that are clearly best suited for one particular conference, which happens to use a closed-access publisher. But that’s why the gods gave us arXiv.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is it appropriate to email to the graduate program chair or coordinator, provide all my academic and professional background and inquire about my eligibility for the program?
Answer: Sure. But don’t expect to read it. If you’re lucky, they’ll send you a pointer to the web pages that describe their admission requirements and their application procedures. If you have a specific question that is not answered on the department’s web site, you’re far better off sending an email asking that specific question. For example, if one of the admission criteria is “an undergraduate degree in computer science or related field”, you might not be certain whether your degree is “related” enough for you to be eligible. But then you should ask that question directly: I am interested in applying to your graduate program, but I have an bachelor’s degree in Applied Eschatology from Miskatonic University, and I’m unsure whether that qualifies as a “related field” to computer science. What criteria do you use to decide whether a non-CS undergraduate degree is “related” enough to computer science to qualify for admission? On the other hand, maybe your real question is “Will I get in if I apply?” I’m sorry, but the graduate program chair doesn’t get to make that determination; that’s the job of the admissions committee. And the only reliable way to ask the admissions committee is by sending them a complete application.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Can I get into a top graduate school for computer science with a 3.6 GPA? What schools would I be eligible for? (I have a decent amount of research experience but all of my research is applying CS to other topics)
Answer: Every top computer science graduate school regularly admits applicants with 3.6 GPAs. Your GPA definitely won’t get you into a top computer science graduate school, because that’s not how anyone gets in, but it won’t keep you out either. Here’s some real data from my own CS department, which has been ranked #5 in the country by US News for more than 20 years. We received more than 1450 applicants for Fall 2023 admission to our PhD program. I sorted these by normalized undergraduate GPA—breaking ties randomly—and partitioned them into 100-student cohorts. Here are GPA ranges and numbers of admission offers for the top 12 cohorts, plus a 13th “cohort” for all lower GPAs. (Yes, we got more than 100 applications with perfect 4.00 GPAs, and yes, we rejected most of them.) All else being equal, a typical applicant with a 3.6 GPA had about 13% chance of admission. For comparison, our overall PhD admission rate this year was about 17%. But of course, not all else is equal. Admissions committees are looking primarily for concrete evidence of research potential. Your research experience should increase your chances, especially if your statement or purpose describes your research efforts in the fluent technical language of active researchers (as opposed to starry-eyed but uninformed “passion”), and you have supportive letters of recommendation that describe your research efforts in credible, technical, and personal detail. The fact that your experience is all in “applying CS to other topics” is not a problem; with the right spin, your expertise outside CS could be sold as a significant advantage.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is arwu, qs, and times, really the top class of uni rankings?
Answer: Oh boy, are we ranking different university rankings, now? Can we rank different ways of ranking the rankings next? There is no ground-truth objective ranking of universities. There is no objective sense in which one university is objectively better or worse than another. One university can be better than another for a particular purpose, but different universities are better for different purposes, and even for the same purpose, the ranking is far more subtle than a linear order. Harvard is one of the best universities in the world for some people, but Harvard is also one of the worst universities in the world for other people. Same for Oxford. Same for Caltech. Same for Tsinghua. Same for ETH Zürich. Same for UC San Diego. Same for Reed College. Same for the University of Montana. Same for Middle Tennessee State University. Same for Lake County Community College. My university ranks #30, #35, #42, #48, #49, #52, #64, #74, or #85, depending on which ranking you consult, and in which year. Within my subject (computer science), my university ranks between #50 and #75, #42, #30, #29, #27, #26, #25, #25, #21, #19, #18, #17, #15, #15, #11, #11, #9, #7, #5, #5, #5, or #2, again depending on which ranking you consult and in which year. (These are a mixture of national and international rankings.) Within my subfield (theoretical computer science), according to the most popular ranking in the US, my department ranked #15 ten years ago, #11 five years ago, and #5 last year. Most of these rankings are based on metrics that track research productivity (publications, grants, student/faculty ratios) and crude metrics of research impact (publications in highly rated venues*, citation counts, major awards, reputation surveys), neither of which have much to do with educational quality or alumni success. Some are based on employment outcomes, but using data sources with wildly varying accuracy (reputation surveys, employment in highly rated companies*, self-reported salaries). Different rankings have different regional/national biases. (*Yes, it’s turtles all the way down.) See, look, here’s ironclad proof that both UC Davis and Illinois are better than Harvard! …along with solid evidence that Illinois truly is the UC Davis of the Midwest. None of these rankings are wrong. They’re just different, because they use different metrics based on different data. In particular, they are all different from the ranking that you really want— regardless of whether you are an aspiring undergraduate, aspiring graduate students, aspiring faculty member, graduate admissions committee, faculty recruiting committee, industry recruiter, or government funding agency. Your career trajectory depends far more on your own interests, priorities, goals, and achievements than on the university you attend.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I know math as a general subject isn't capitalized, and Algebra 1 would be due to being a course title, but what about when a general subject (such as precalculus) stands alone as a course title?
Answer: It depends on how you’re using the word. If you are using the noun to refer to a particular course, it should be capitalized. “Prof. Smith is teaching Precalculus this semester.” If you are using the noun to refer to the general subfield, it should not be capitalized. “I really wish my Calculus students were better at precalculus.” The difference can be subtle. Consider “I am taking Precalculus” (the class) versus “I am studying precalculus” (the subject). Or consider “I am studying for a Precalculus exam” (an exam in a class called Precalculus) versus “I am studying for a precalculus exam” (an exam on the topic of precalculus).

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How do you determine if an author has submitted the same manuscript to multiple journals?
Answer: The usual method is to ask highly qualified experts on the specific, narrow topic of the paper to referee that paper. For most research papers, the number of highly qualified experts is actually quite small—typically less than twenty, sometimes less than five. So if an author has submitted the same paper to multiple journals, and the editor of each submitted journal asks three of those experts for a referee report, there is a fair to good chance that the same expert will be asked for a referee report more than once. At least in the fields I work in, submitting the same paper to multiple journals at the same time is considered extremely unethical. Journal editors and referees (and in computer science, conference program committee members and reviewers) are unpaid volunteers, who offer their utterly necessary necessary services to benefit the research community, and to pay back people who reviewed their papers in the past. Their time and energy are limited resources. In the end, only one journal can accept and print the paper; parallel submissions complete waste all but one journal’s time and effort. If you submit the same paper to multiple journals and get caught, your paper is very likely to be desk-rejected from both journals, and those journals are likely to bar you from submitting again, at least for a few years. Just don’t.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is a systematic approach to come up with a research topic that can be published in a top CS conference?
Answer: You’re asking the wrong question. Research topics aren’t published in top CS conferences. Research results are published in top CS conferences. (Strictly speaking, even that’s not correct—research papers are published in top CS conferences. But those papers are judged primarily on the strength and novelty of their results. It’s not enough to be about a relevant and interesting topic.) But the answer is still NO. If anyone knew of a truly systematic approach to develop research results that would be published in a top CS conference, that approach would quickly be automated, the resulting software would be used to flood that conference with results, and the conference would be ruined for mere humans. In short, that particular research area would be driven into irrelevant oblivion; researchers would move on to more interesting topics.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Who are some famous professors in the field of computer science who are ready to meet random software engineers relevant to the professors' field of study/doubts/technical discussion and work with them/work in their research and development?
Answer: You’re joking, right? Let’s set aside the low probability of a random software engineer being relevant to a famous computer scientist’s field of study. With rare exceptions, the only people relevant to a computer science professor’s field of study are other professional computer science researchers. Famous people, just like non-famous people, value their time and their privacy. They have lives and jobs and families and students (often in the hundreds). Even the Blessed Keanu Himself, despite his boundless generosity and humility, wouldn’t be willing to meet random strangers and give them acting / martial arts / bass guitar / motorcycle maintenance / sudoku lessons. And even if he were, it would be rude of you to ask him.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is the maximum length of a substring that occurs twice in a given string?
Answer: That depends on the given string, obviously. The maximum answer over all strings of length n is exactly n − 1 . For example, the string AAAAAA occurs exactly twice as a substring of AAAAAAA. The minimum answer over all strings of length n is exactly 0. The empty string is the only string that appears more than once as a substring of STRING.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How can I publish a research paper on my own without my professor's help? Which journal should I choose as a communication major?
Answer: How can I publish a research paper on my own without my professor's help? Choose a journal to submit to. (See below.) Follow the submission instructions on the journal’s web site, and follow them precisely. Wait for the referee reports. If your paper is rejected, revise it to address any concerns raised in the referee reports and resubmit it to a different journal (restarting the process). If your paper is not rejected, revise it as directed by the editor, in response to concerns raised in the referee reports. Curse Referee #2. Repeat until the editor accepts the paper. Read the galley proofs extremely carefully, because the copy editor will introduce significant errors. Submit the corrected galley proofs. Sign the copyright transfer form / publication agreement. Wait for the paper to appear on the publisher’s web site. In other words, exactly the same way as your advisor (and everyone else) would do it. Which journal should I choose as a communication major? That obviously depends on the content and intended audience of your paper, but as a general rule of thumb, I recommend submitting to the journal that your paper cites the most.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is your opinion regarding one going directly from undergraduate CS to master’s? Is it preferred by schools like CMU and Stanford that one have some work experience first?
Answer: What is your opinion regarding one going directly from undergraduate CS to master’s? Honestly, when I read the first sentence of your question, my first thought was “As opposed to what?!” I think most master’s students, at least in my department, apply directly as undergraduates. But that’s just a hypothesis. Let’s see if the actual data supports it! My department has two on-campus master’s degree programs: a research-based “Master of Science” (MS) and a terminal course-based “Master of Computer Science” (MCS). For each of these programs, we received about 2700 applications for Fall 2024 admission. Here are Fall 2024 acceptance numbers for the MS program, broken out by the year of the applicant’s undergraduate degree. The largest number of applications, the largest number of acceptances, and the largest fraction of acceptances are all from 2024; those applicants were all undergraduates when they applied. And here is the corresponding data for the (on-campus) MCS program. Again, the largest number of applications, the largest number of acceptances, and the largest acceptance rate were all for current undergraduates expecting to get their bachelor’s degrees in 2024. Applying in the first year after graduation is almost as good, but applying more than one year later seems to hurt significantly. tl;dr: Actual admission data supports the hypothesis that work experience is not a significant advantage, and may be a significant disadvantage, in applying to master’s programs at top CS programs in the US. In hindsight, this shouldn’t be too surprising. Admissions decisions are largely based on evidence that the applicant is prepared for graduate-level coursework and (for MS applicants) research. As a rule, graduate-level classes assume a strong undergraduate academic background. Research also requires a song academic background. The more time you spend away from school, the spongier your academic skills get. The skills that people develop with work experience are valuable and important for success in the professional world, but for most people, they are different. All that said, remember that every department makes its own graduate admissions decisions using its own criteria. If you really want to learn what a department looks for in its master’s-degree applicants, the best way to find out is to call the department’s graduate admissions office and ask them.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How intelligent is artificial intelligence? Do I have to plug it in for it to work or does it power itself from within itself like naturally-occurring biologically rendered forms of universal electromagnetism? Are there quantum entanglements?
Answer: How intelligent is artificial intelligence? It’s not. It’s mostly fiction. Do I have to plug it in for it to work I assume you’re referring to the computers that so-called AI software runs on. (Do you need to feed English for it to work? No, English is not the kind of thing that can be fed. You don’t need to feed English books, but you do need to feed English speakers and English writers and English readers.) Whether you need to “plug it in” depends on the device. Many computers run on batteries. You might need to plug them in when the battery charge gets low, or you might need to attach them to another source of energy (like a running gasoline engine), or you might need to replace the old batteries with new ones. But every modern computer does require electricity. or does it power itself from within itself No. The second law of thermodynamics prevents that, for the same reason that it prevents perpetual motion. Batteries only work until they run out of charge, and every battery will eventually run out of charge. like naturally-occurring biologically rendered forms of universal electromagnetism? Wow. That is an impressive word salad. You should consider getting more sleep. Living things do not “power themselves from within themselves.” Living things need to get energy from the outside world, or they die. Plants get energy from the sun. Animals get energy by eating plants and other animals. Anyone using the phrase “universal electromagnetism” seriously is either deeply misinformed or is trying to scam you. Or both. Are there quantum entanglements? Yes, quantum entanglement exists, but it has absolutely nothing to do with AI. You might as well ask if there is gravity.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How prevalent is plagiarism among undergraduate students at American universities and colleges?
Answer: Roughly 20–30% of American undergraduates plagiarize at least once. Contrary to what another answer says, we actually have a lot of data about this, thanks largely to the research of Donald McCabe and his colleagues. The following table appears in this 2001 survey of over a decade of academic integrity research. Each column shows the percentage of surveyed students—each from multiple institutions—who admitted to having committed each type of academic misconduct at least once. The 1990–91 and 1995–96 studies separated responses from universities with honor codes and those without. Obviously there is no way to know how many students plagiarized but didn’t admit to plagiarism in the survey. More recent statistics are presumably available in this 2022 book by Rettinger and Gallant, but I don’t have access to a legal online copy (cough). But everyone should also be aware of the following “plea bargaining” study. Study participants were told that the study was about group versus individual problem solving. Pairs of students were put into rooms; each pair was given a sequence of logic problems to solve together, followed by another sequence of logic problems to solve individually. In each room, only one student was actually a subject; the other was part of the research team. In half of the rooms, during the individual-work phase, the researcher asked the subject cheating questions like “What did you get for problem 2?”. The (small!) number of students who ignored these questions were removed from the study. In the other half of the room, the researcher stayed quiet; none of the subjects asked cheating questions. After the second test phase, the subjects — whether innocent or guilty — were accused of cheating and offered a plea deal. If they admitted cheating, they would lose the reward for participating in the study, and that would end the matter; if they refused to admit cheating, they woudl be reported to the university’s Academic Review Board. Over half of the innocent students admitted to cheating.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Why do we use the non-deterministic algorithm to solve an optimization problem?
Answer: First of all, there is more than one non-deterministic algorithm. So I think your question is asking “Why do we use non-deterministic algorithms to solve optimization problems?” And the answer is: We don’t! We use non-deterministic algorithms to prove theorems about optimization problems. Non-determinism is a mathematical abstraction. It is not a technique that one can actually use to solve optimization problems (or any other type of problem) in the real world.

Question: Can I do a double major and a triple minor at the same time?
Answer: Mayyybe. But dear gods, why would you want to? Nobody but you, your parents, and possibly your significant other are going to be impressed with how many bureaucratic hurdles you jumped. That extra major and all those minors aren’t going to get you into a better graduate school or hired into a better job. You’re more likely to be labeled a eternal student / dilettante than a polymath / genius. Pick a major. Take classes outside that major interest you. Focus on building the skills and expertise that those classes teach. Jump the bureaucratic hurdles for a minor or a second major only if taking the classes you want to take is impossible otherwise. Most importantly, learn to learn on your own, without the structure of classes or a major, so that you can continue learning for decades after you graduate.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Have you ever seen a student's willingness to sacrifice/jeopardize high grades/GPA (e.g., taking harder classes outside their "comfort zone"; unusual research projects/extra-curriculars) pay off intellectually, academically, or in career trajectory?
Answer: YES. In fact, I think this description applies to a significant majority of successful people that I’ve met during my 30-something years in academia. (Admittedly, it’s not always easy to tell. A small minority of super-strong students take significant risks, taking harder classes well outside their comfort zone, and still manage to get nothing but As.) I have also seen plenty of 4.0-GPA students completely flounder outside the narrow confines of academia, where all problems have relatively short, relatively simple, well-structured solutions that only use techniques that can be taught in a single term, and that an expert can solve in at most a few days. This isn’t just my personal opinion. My (top-5 US computer science) department’s PhD program rejects a significant majority of applicants with perfect undergraduate grades, even when they come from stellar departments like MIT, Berkeley, Stanford, or CMU. We’d much rather admit a student with a 3.0 GPA and a strong research portfolio than a student with a 4.0 GPA who has done nothing else.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I am currently a PhD student at the University of Michigan - Dearborn. Is there any opportunity for me to transfer to study at the main campus, University of Michigan - Ann Arbor?
Answer: There is no such thing as “transferring” from one PhD program to another. Even if you accepted admission to the PhD program in Ann Arbor, you would be starting your PhD over from scratch (possibly except for a few classes). If you all want to do is study in Ann Arbor, all you need to do is (1) drive to Ann Arbor and then (2) study. It’s very likely that the University of Michigan system shares library privileges between campuses, and there are coffee shops and Google everywhere. If you what you really want is to work with faculty at Ann Arbor, you can do certainly that, exactly the same way that you would work with faculty in East Lansing or Madison or Austin or Münich—networking. Go to conferences in your chosen field of study. Drive to Ann Arbor (or join a Zoom broadcast) and attend seminars in your subfield; volunteer to give a talk; give a really good talk. Ask your PhD advisor to introduce you to colleagues that share your research interests. If a research collaboration naturally evolves, congratulations! (Do not attempt to do this without the support of your PhD advisor in Dearborn.) If what you really want is a PhD from UM Ann Arbor, the only way to get that is to apply and to be admitted, just like you were at Dearborn, and then do the work, just like you’re doing at Dearborn.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is UIUC MSCS more competitive than their PhD program, considering both provide funding?
Answer: Here are some statistics about graduate applications in computer science at UIUC, for the Fall 2023 admissions cycle: Previous years’ application and admission rates are similar. So in terms of raw selectivity, yes, the MSCS program is more competitive. There are significantly more MSCS applicants than PhD applicants, and significantly fewer MCSC admission offers than PhD admission offers, so the admission rate for the MSCS program is significantly lower than for the PhD program. That doesn’t necessarily mean that your chances of admission would be significantly lower for the MSCS program than for the PhD program. First, a lot of self-selection goes into these applications; the application pools are different. Students who are less sure about liking research, or who are aiming at careers in industry, or who just don’t want to spend 5–7 more years in school are more likely to apply to the MSCS program. Second, the two programs look for different profiles of students; the admissions criteria are different. MS admissions are based more on coursework and potential for incremental research contributions in a relatively short time frame; PhD admissions are based more on potential to grow into a successful independent researcher over several years.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How do I know if my research is high quality? (Math)
Answer: Write it up. Give the writeup to a mathematician you trust (their expertise, their ethics, and their opinions/taste). Then trust them. If you are a student, the trusted mathematician is usually a math professor at your university. In particular, if you are a graduate student, the trusted mathematician is usually your advisor or another faculty mentor. If you already have a network of collaborators, the trusted mathematician could be one of them. If all else fails, the trusted mathematician could be the editor of a journal (and the process is called submission).

Question: MY Ph.D. advisor admitted he/she wronged me by taking away credit. What should I do about it?

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: If logic gives meaning to the universe, how can scientific materialists explain the existence of the logical laws that govern it?
Answer: Pardon me, sir. What kind of dressing would you like on your word salad? Logic does not give meaning to the universe. The universe doesn’t have meaning, for the same reason that cats cannot be prime, or that black holes cannot vote for Trump. The universe isn’t even the kind of thing that can have meaning. You’re thinking of language. The universe is not a word, or a sentence, or a novel, or even an encyclopedia. Logical laws do not govern the universe. The universe is not governed by laws. The things we call “laws” in the context of science and mathematics are not the kinds of things that can be governed with. Scientific laws describe the universe, or more accurately, vastly simplified but useful models of the universe. Logical laws don’t even do that much, because logic isn’t about the universe at all; it’s about the language that we use to talk about the universe (or more accurately, our vastly simplified models thereof). De Morgan’s law says nothing about black holes or quantum entanglement. Protons don’t go to jail for violating modus ponens. Logic gives structure to the language that we use to talk about (models of) the universe. The laws of logic exist because we humans find them useful to talk about (models of) the universe.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: A faculty told his/her grad students in his lab that their thoughts cannot override his thoughts. He/she asked them to leave the lab if they can’t follow this rule. What should students do?
Answer: Leave the lab. Run, don’t walk. A student’s thoughts can absolutely override a professor’s thoughts, if the experimental data is more consistent with the student’s thoughts than the professor’s. If the professor doesn’t recognize this basic scientific tenet, they are either scientifically or ethically unqualified to advise PhD students.

Question: In the introduction section of my research paper, can I write my own background based on my knowledge of the topic, or do I have to rely on what other researchers have said?
Answer: Both!! Almost by definition, everything you write is based on your own knowledge of the topic. That’s what writing is—communicating your knowledge to other people. On the other hand, your readers have no reason to trust you You need to convince them that you know what you’re talking about. You need to justify any claims you make, even in the introduction, either by direct reasoning (based on premises that must be justified, recursively) or by citing the appropriate literature. You also need to give proper credit for any ideas or results or techniques you describe, even in the introduction. You also need to provide pointers to relevant background material that doesn’t make sense to include directly, so that novice readers can understand your results. You need to set your work in its proper context, especially in the introduction, by comparing it to existing work. In short, you should write the background section based on your own knowledge of the topic, which already relies on the work of others, but you should also make that reliance explicit.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is the review of Purdue University Indy campus for engineering? Is it going to be more similar to Purdue University West Lafayette or more IUPUI?
Answer: [Someone who actually works at Purdue should sanity-check this answer; I’m writing from one state over.] Nobody knows yet. IUPUI formally ceases to exist on July 1, 2024. The programs at IUPUI that are administered by the Purdue system, including all engineering programs, are being rebranded as Purdue University in Indianapolis; programs administered by the Indiana University system are being rebranded as Indiana University Indianapolis. PUI advertises that it will offer exactly the same programs, with exactly the same classes and learning goals, as the Purdue West Lafayette campus. I’m skeptical. PUI students will be able to take in-person classes in Indy and online classes offered by Purdue faculty in West Lafayette. Eventually, PUI students may be allowed to commute an hour to West Lafayette to take in-person classes there, but not for at least a few years. But If I were to hazard a guess: The students at Purdue West Lafayette are significantly stronger than the students at Purdue Indianapolis, and that difference will persist for at least a decade. Purdue West Lafayette is known as a world-class engineering school. Purdue in Indianapolis is not. No matter how the university might protest otherwise, everyone still knows that the real Purdue is in West Lafayette. So West Lafayette is likely to attract a much stronger applicant pool than Indianapolis. The same dynamics will play out among the faculty as well—after the embarassing “university tenure” smoke clears—but I think that’s less significant. It’s the students, more than the faculty, that make Purdue such an engineering powerhouse. Well-taught university classes are calibrated to match the backgrounds and skills of the students that take them. If the Purdue West Lafayette faculty have stronger students on average, they will teach harder classes, because the students will demand them. If the Purdue Indianapolis faculty have weaker students on average, they will teach easier classes, because the students will require them. And that’s true even for classes that have identical catalog descriptions, identical advertised learning goals, identical textbooks, and even identical lectures. (Note well: “stronger” and “weaker” do not mean “smarter” and “dumber”, but rather “more prepared” and “less prepared”.) In the long run, the difference between the two Purdue campuses might even out, or even reverse, but I’m not holding my breath. tl;dr: More IUPUI, because that’s what PUI actually is.

Question: Is it possible to take classes at a community/junior college as a way to potentially boost my GPA even though I already have a Bachelor’s degree? If so, how exactly does it work and could it help me into grad school?
Answer: No. GPAs do not average across institutions or degree programs. You have a bachelor’s degree. Your undergraduate GPA will never change. You are done. You can enroll in community college courses, and your grades in those courses will establish a new GPA at the community college, but that won’t change your undergraduate GPA. Even if you enroll in a new degree program at your old undergraduate university, you will have a new GPA within that new degree program.

Question: ? Hey my love . Im in big problem 😞 could u help me / my professor wants from me to write a research composed of 20 pages 😞 I can’t do it . My topic is (speech community) please 😞 help me if u have a research about it or any thing?
Answer: Yes, you can. No, really. You can. Maybe not right away. Maybe not even by the time your professor’s assignment is due, but yes, you can write a 20-page research paper on “speech community”. The trick is to start by writing one page, or even one paragraph, or even just two sentences, about any topic. Write about literally anything. Get guidance and feedback from your professors, from your teaching assistants, from the writing/tutoring center if your school has one, or even from your peers. Watch your spelling and grammar and punctuation, and keep the emojis to a minimum 🙁. Stick to a single topic. Tell a story. That’s all writing is—telling a story. Once you’re more comfortable writing one page, write two. Once you’re more comfortable writing two pages, write five. Once you’re more comfortable writing five pages, write ten. Once you’re more comfortable writing ten pages, write twenty. Meanwhile, you also need practice learning to do research. Again, the best people to give you guidance and feedback are your teachers, your writing/tutoring center, and your librarians. Research involves a lot of reading, and a lot of taking notes and organizing information, but those are also skills that you can develop with practice. Learn a story about what you want to write about. That’s all research is—learning a story. But by far the most important thing about learning writing — or any other skill, like cooking, or dancing, or carpentry, or basketball, or interviewing for jobs, or flirting, or parenting — is that you have to do the work yourself. You have to try, you have to fail, you have to try again, you have to get help, you have to try again. The only way to learn to do the thing is to actually do the thing. Your other questions strongly suggest that you are taking a university-level class in linguistics. Since you’re taking a class that is asking for a 20-page research paper, you’ve already had opportunities to learn reading and writing and research skills, so you don’t need to start from scratch. And you were admitted based on your past academic record; the admissions committee was convinced that you can succeed at their university, if you take advantage of the opportunity to practice. Good luck!

Question: What is the Chomsky normal form (CNF) of a Turing machine?
Answer: There’s no such thing. Chomsky normal form is a type of context-free grammar. Turing machines are not context-free grammars.

Question: Can I get accepted in an economic PhD if I have already done a biology PhD but not an economics undergraduate degree?
Answer: Probably not. You already have a PhD, so you already know how to do research—how to identify and read relevant literature, how to formulate a testable hypothesis, how to teach yourself unfamiliar concepts or techniques, how to “read the room” (by reading the literature) to understand whether your research problem is interesting, how to design and perform experiments, how to analyze data, how to learn how to write for your audience, how to respond to Referee #2, and so on. Yes, the specifics differ from one field to the next, but that’s just a matter of degree—the specifics also vary from one problem to the next. If you don’t have a strong enough economics background to succeed in an economics PhD program, then you won’t succeed in an economics PhD program. If you do have a strong enough economics background to succeed in an economics PhD program, you don’t need an economics PhD. Just start doing economics research.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is it better to write a technical book instead of several research papers?
Answer: [A2A] Answering as a computer science professor: Not if you want tenure! The standard expectations for hiring and promoting faculty in most (if not all) fields of science and engineering include publishing research papers in peer-reviewed venues. In most fields that means refereed journals; in most subfields of computer science, that means competitive peer-reviewed conference proceedings. These venues are where the research community expect to see research results; publishing in these values is the easiest way to build both a public record of your research accomplishments and your reputation as a researcher. (Expectations in other disciplines are different, especially in the humanities.) It’s the easiest way not because it’s easy, but because that’s how everybody expects it to be done, so that’s where everyone’s attention already is. Hiring committees are going to look first at your publication record. Promotion committees are going to look first at your publication record. The people writing evaluation letters for your promotion case are going to look first at your publication record. Rule Number One in dealing with committees that might evaluate you for anything: Thou Shalt Not Give the Committee an Excuse to Think. Publishing a book instead of several papers is non-standard,.and doing anything nonstandard gives the hiring/promotions committee an Excuse to Think. You will be held to a more stringent standard, because people are generally skeptical about unfamiliar things, and [whining] thinking is haaaaaaard. Some committee members will just want to reflexively reject anything “weird”, so other committee members will have argue more strongly to convince them. Now, I’m not saying that it’s impossible to establish a strong enough reputation by writing a book to be hired and tenured. I’ve seen it work, but it’s rare. I don’t recommend the risk.

Question: What are the fields of "computational algebraic geometry", "computational geometry", and "computational game theory" and what do they study?
Answer: Computational geometry is the study of algorithms and data structures for problems where the input has a natural interpretation as points, lines, planes, circles, spheres, line segments, polygons, axis-aligned boxes, or other simple (typically low-dimensional) geometric objects. Here are some typical problems: Computational geometry is primarily concerned with objects that have linear or piecewise-linear descriptions, such as polyhedra with flat faces. Computational algebraic geometry deals with geometric problems where the objects are best described with higher- (but still low-) degree polynomials. Problems of this form arise naturally in the study of (inverse) kinematics and visibility, even when the underlying physical objects are piecewise-linear. (Beware, this stuff gets really complex really quickly.) Algorithmic game theory is the study of algorithmic problems for competing strategic agents, for example, players in a game, bidders in an auction, candidates in an election, or children fighting over a birthday cake. Game theory does have some overlap with geometry—or more accurately topology—in the form of certain fixed-point theorems.
